flags.quote: Embedded real-time control: designed and implemented a 1 kHz PI velocity controller in C++ on an ESP32-S3 (FreeRTOS), model-based tuned with feed-forward and anti-windup (0.8% speed error in simulation), with 10 fault monitors, a hardware watchdog, and a kill switch.
flags.issue: The lead-in 'Embedded real-time control' plus 'on an ESP32-S3' tells the reader this loop runs on a microcontroller. It has never run on any ESP32. The v2 board it targets is schematic-only, and the code has only executed inside a host-side simulator. 'In simulation' is attached only to the 0.8%, so the 1 kHz rate, the 10 fault monitors, the hardware watchdog and the kill switch all read as bench-proven. An Apptronik 'real-time controls' interviewer's first question ('worst-case loop time on the S3? what did the watchdog do at bring-up?') has no answer, and the portfolio linked in the header says outright 'not from the board'. The 0.8% also has no condition: it comes from one test, lifting the forearm at 15 deg/s, against 98% for feed-forward alone. Other simulation tests give different numbers.
flags.source_check: firmware/README.md: 'Status: designed and verified in simulation. It has not run on the board yet: the v2 PCB isn't fabricated.' CI only compiles the sketch for the ESP32-S3. index.html: 'every firmware and decoder number below comes from simulation or emulation driven by real recorded EMG, not from the board.' FACTS OR2/OR3/OR5/OR8, the truth guard, and the 'Never claim' list (hardware validation of the v2 board, firmware numbers measured on hardware). The master (U) does say 'implemented ... on an ESP32-S3', so the words are the master's own. The overclaim comes from the added 'Embedded real-time' label and from scoping the simulation qualifier to a single number.
flags.fix: Control firmware: designed and implemented a 1 kHz PI velocity controller in C++17 for an ESP32-S3 (FreeRTOS), tuned from a first-order motor model with feed-forward and anti-windup, with 10 fault monitors, a hardware watchdog and a kill switch; in closed-loop simulation, 0.8% speed error lifting the forearm vs. 98% with feed-forward alone. (Change 'on' to 'for', drop 'Embedded real-time', and make the simulation qualifier cover the whole bullet. It's about the same length, 3 lines.)

flags.issue: This puts the label 'real-time' on a simulated-robot project that has no target hardware. The 20 µs is the median of a benchmark on a cloud Xeon VM running a non-RT kernel. The worst case was 4.0 ms (4x the 1 ms budget), p99 was 60 µs, and 0.135% of deadlines were missed. 'What's your worst case?' is the question he won't want. The closed-loop walking runs also used the Python filter, not the C++ loop, so the 'real-time' filter isn't the one the controllers ran on. The word 'update.' also sits alone on a wasted line.
flags.source_check: quadruped-eskf/results/timing.json: compute p50 18.2 µs, p99 60.5 µs, max 4005 µs, deadline_miss_pct 0.135, note 'non-RT kernel (cloud VM)'. claims.json step_time: 'C++ step about 20 µs of the 1 ms budget (median)'. python/qeskf/closed_loop.py imports the Python Eskf. FACTS LR3.
flags.fix: '...IMU-only; C++ step ~20 µs median of the 1 ms budget.' Drop 'real-time'. This also removes the orphaned 'update.' line, which pays for the longer fixes below.

flags.issue: This is a skill claim with no hardware behind it. Nothing on the page has run on an embedded target, in real time or otherwise. It's the third 'real-time' on the page (skills, the orthosis lead-in, the quadruped update), and all three are simulation or host runs. flags.quote: cut EMG-to-motion latency from 103 ms to 43 ms with a Bayesian EMG estimator, validated in closed-loop simulation on real recorded EMG with 26 GoogleTest tests in CI.
flags.issue: (1) It credits one component for the whole gain. The 43 ms configuration also adds a 20 ms onset confirm and switches to the fast tuning tier (500 deg/s^2 ramp, lambda 30 ms vs. 150 deg/s^2, lambda 50 ms), so 'with a Bayesian EMG estimator' over-attributes. (2) The 103 ms baseline is his own first firmware version, a 2-pole envelope, not an external benchmark. (3) It's a name-drop: the estimator is Sanger's published 2007 method, and 'a Bayesian EMG estimator' invites 'derive it' and 'is it yours?'. He needs the 64-level, Laplacian-likelihood details ready. (4) 'Validated ... with 26 GoogleTest tests' ties the whole suite to this claim, but only Latency.RealEmgOnsetToMotion pins latency. The other 25 cover the decoder, estimator, PI, closed loop and safety. The figures come from 24 contractions (p90 82 ms).
flags.source_check: firmware/README.md latency table: 'First version (2-pole 4 Hz, 150 deg/s^2, lambda 50 ms) 103 ms' vs. 'Now (Bayesian, 20 ms confirm, fast tier) 43 ms (p90 82)'; 'A Bayesian amplitude estimator (Sanger 2007)'; 'The test Latency.RealEmgOnsetToMotion pins these numbers in CI'. FACTS OR5, OR6 ('with a Bayesian EMG amplitude estimator and a 20 ms onset confirm ... Stop lag went from 89 ms to 32 ms').
flags.fix: Signal processing: cut EMG-to-motion latency from 103 ms to 43 ms (stop lag 89 to 32 ms) with a Bayesian EMG amplitude estimator and a 20 ms onset confirm, in closed-loop simulation driven by real recorded EMG; 26 GoogleTest unit, closed-loop and latency tests run in CI. Needs Troy: confirm whether the fast-tier retune is part of the 43 ms. If it is, add 'and a retuned loop'.

flags.quote: redesigned the 4-channel EMG board in KiCad (INA333, right-leg drive, ISO7763 isolation), raising cross-day gesture decoding from 31% to 87% in emulation.
flags.issue: (1) Status: 'redesigned the board' reads as a built, working board. v2 is schematic-complete only, with no layout, no fabrication and no power-up. (2) Weak baseline: 31% is the emulated v1 front end, whose unbuffered inputs and diode peak detector pass almost nothing (only 0.22% of samples clear the diode). A skeptic hears 'fixed a broken board', and the 31-to-87 jump looks inflated. The defensible claim is the ceiling: 87.3% vs. 87.9% with no board at all. (3) Conditions are missing: 11 classes, 115 days of real EMG. (4) 'Raising decoding' credits a board with accuracy that no hardware has produced.
flags.source_check: FACTS OR8: 'The v2 schematic is complete. Layout and fabrication come next. v1 was fabricated.' OR9: '115 days ... 87.3% vs. an 87.9% ceiling with no board.' orthosis-emg-decoder/README.md, 'Why v1 fails': 'only 0.22 % of samples ever clear the diode'. Buffered, v1 reaches 59.5-71.4%.
flags.fix: Led a 5-engineer team; redesigned the 4-channel EMG board schematic in KiCad (INA333, right-leg drive, ISO7763 isolation); in emulation on 115 days of real EMG, cross-day 11-class decoding rose from 31% (v1) to 87%, within a point of the 87.9% no-board ceiling.

flags.quote: with 0 falls in 5 × 60 s walks (QP after a 4 s startup turn); the QP controller cut ground-truth velocity-tracking error from 0.169 to 0.091 m/s.
flags.issue: (1) The baseline isn't named. 0.169 m/s is Troy's own scripted position-servo trot, which his README calls 'loose', yet 'cut ... from 0.169' reads as beating a real controller. (2) 'Ground-truth velocity-tracking error' is ambiguous. It means the controller was fed ground truth, but a reader can take it for the result on the estimate. (3) The parenthetical begs 'why a startup turn?'. The answer is the project's best engineering story (tilt is weakly observable on a straight walk, which caused a ~4 deg lean), and it was cut, so the turn now reads like a hack. Without the turn the QP fell in 1 of 5 runs. (4) The sample is 5 seeds of one flat-ground walk at 0.2-0.45 m/s.
flags.source_check: quadruped-eskf/README.md: 'scripted trot' is the walking controller; 'controller's own tracking error (0.17 m/s, mostly the loose scripted trot)'; QP falls '1 / 5 fed the estimate (seed 3, t = 7.0 s); 0 / 5 ... after a 4 s turn at startup'; Limitations: '0.2-0.45 m/s'. FACTS LR7, LR8, LR9 ('0.091 m/s vs. 0.169 m/s for the scripted trot (fed ground truth)').
flags.fix: Control: walking and 500 Hz QP force-balance controllers ran on the estimate with 0 falls in 5 × 60 s walks; found tilt only weakly observable on straight walks (~4° lean) and fixed it with a 4 s startup turn, which the QP needs. Fed ground truth, the QP tracked velocity to 0.091 m/s vs. 0.169 m/s for the scripted trot. (About +1 line, covered by the orphan line saved in flag 2.)

flags.quote: Developing rigid-body kinematics and dynamics for Atlas impacts: floating-base forward kinematics (quaternions, Rodrigues' rotations, velocity composition) from joint encoders maps impacts onto the robot mesh, and Khatib's operational-space effective mass estimates impact energy.
flags.issue: (1) Name-drop on proprietary work. A humanoid interviewer will say 'write Lambda = (J M^-1 J^T)^-1: whose mass matrix, which Jacobian, which contact point, and where does delta-v come from?' The answers touch Boston Dynamics internals he may not be allowed to discuss. (2) As written, the method is physically incomplete. Effective mass alone gives no energy; the master pairs it with an OLS velocity fit, and this version cut that. (3) Scope inflation: 'developing rigid-body kinematics and dynamics for Atlas' sounds like owning Atlas's dynamics model. The work is impact analysis: forward kinematics on encoder data plus an effective-mass estimate. (4) 'Rodrigues' rotations' isn't a term (it's Rodrigues' rotation formula), and stacking three rotation buzzwords reads as keyword padding.
flags.source_check: FACTS BD1 ('Maps impacts onto the robot's mesh using encoders and forward kinematics'), BD2 ('Estimates impact energy from Khatib's operational-space effective mass and an OLS velocity fit'), BD4 ('Rodrigues' rotation formula'; 'exact rigid-body velocity composition'). The master: 'Mapping impacts ... estimating their energy from Khatib's operational-space effective mass and an OLS velocity fit, and building a physics-based MuJoCo impact simulation.' FACTS: 'Keep it proprietary-safe: method only.'
flags.fix: Mapping impacts onto Atlas's mesh with floating-base forward kinematics from joint encoders (quaternions, Rodrigues' formula, rigid-body velocity composition), estimating impact energy from operational-space effective mass and an OLS velocity fit, and building a physics-based MuJoCo impact simulation. Keep 'Khatib's' only if Troy can derive Lambda on a whiteboard without BD specifics.

top3: The orthosis bullet leads with 'Embedded real-time control ... on an ESP32-S3', and the skills list 'real-time embedded'. The firmware has never run on any hardware: the v2 board isn't fabricated, and every number comes from a host simulator, as the linked portfolio says. Retitle it 'Control firmware', write 'for an ESP32-S3', put 'in closed-loop simulation' over the whole bullet with the 0.8% vs. 98% feed-forward-only baseline, and drop 'real-time' from the skills.

Several numbers lack honest baselines and conditions. '~20 µs per real-time update' is a median on a non-RT cloud VM (worst case 4 ms). The QP's 0.169 to 0.091 m/s is measured against his own loose scripted trot, fed ground truth. 31% to 87% compares against a v1 front end that was effectively broken, so lead with 87.3% vs. the 87.9% no-board ceiling and say 'schematic'. 103 to 43 ms is credited to the Bayesian estimator alone, though the 20 ms onset confirm and the loop tuning also changed. Name each baseline, and restore the tilt-observability reason for the startup turn.

Credit, causality and name-drops invite questions he may not want. At Caterpillar, were the 4.7% and 3.3% team results, and were they measured or projected? (Needs Troy.) At Boston Dynamics, 'Khatib's operational-space effective mass estimates impact energy' drops the OLS velocity fit, which makes the method physically incomplete, and invites proprietary probing. 'Bayesian EMG estimator' is Sanger's published method. The header's 'code' link leads to no code, and the site still shows GPA 3.4. Point the header at github.com/tmayer2112-ui/Troy_Mayer and re-sync the site.
